structure.title: I
structure.summary: In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway arrives in West Egg and rents a modest eighty-dollar bungalow, settling alone after his roommate is transferred to Washington; he acquires an old Dodge, a Finnish housekeeper, and briefly a dog that runs away, initially feeling isolated until a stranger’s request for directions makes him feel like a local guide. He buys twelve volumes on banking and investment as symbols of future success and drives to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale, where they reside in a lavish Georgian mansion overlooking the bay. During dinner, Tom aggressively espouses racist pseudoscience from 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' while Daisy and Jordan Baker respond with detached irony; a phone call reveals Tom’s affair in New York, which Jordan confirms to Nick, and Daisy bitterly wishes her daughter be a 'beautiful little fool,' as the evening dissolves into artificial rituals like pointless candle-relighting. After leaving, Nick drives home to West Egg, reflecting on Daisy’s emotional detachment and Tom’s depression, before seeing Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light at the end of a dock, only for Gatsby to vanish into the night.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where they disembark and enter George Wilson’s run-down garage to meet Tom’s mistress, Myrtle Wilson. Tom insists Nick accompany them to New York, and they board separate train cars to avoid scrutiny; in the city, Myrtle purchases a white-footed Airedale puppy and takes a lavender taxicab to her cramped, overcrowded apartment on 158th Street, where she hosts an afternoon gathering with her sister Catherine and neighbors Mr. and Mrs. McKee, serving whisky. As alcohol flows freely, Myrtle boasts about meeting Tom on a train while pretending to be refined, declares her intentions to buy luxuries including a massage, a dog collar, and a wreath for her mother’s grave, and defiantly shouts Daisy’s name—prompting Tom to violently break her nose, triggering chaos as women scramble to tend to her injury with bloodied towels and Mr. McKee stumbles out the door. Overwhelmed, Nick leaves with McKee in the elevator and later awakens exhausted and alone in the cold lower level of Pennsylvania Station, waiting for the four o’clock train.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway arriving by car at Jay Gatsby’s mansion on Long Island just after seven on a Saturday evening, where a lavish, chaotic party unfolds amid music, champagne, and extravagant displays including five crates of weekly fruit deliveries and an eight-piece orchestra in the garden. Amid rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick Carraway meets Jordan Baker and observes absurd displays of wealth, including a drunken guest’s awe at Gatsby’s real books with uncut pages; later, Nick Carraway unknowingly converses with Gatsby himself, who reveals his identity, invites him to fly in a hydroplane the next morning, and speaks of his Oxford background—a claim Jordan doubts. As the party peaks past midnight with opera singers, drunken outbursts, marital quarrels, and a car crash caused by Owl-Eyed Man crashing Gatsby’s new coupé into a wall, Gatsby remains detached and sober, while Nick Carraway witnesses Jordan being called away for a private hour-long conversation with him; the chapter closes as Nick Carraway leaves, finding Gatsby alone on the porch waving farewell under a faint moon, the party’s energy dissolving into isolation. In reflection, Nick recounts his daily life in New York—working at the Probity Trust, dining with clerks, studying investments at the Yale Club, and walking home along Madison Avenue and 33rd Street to Pennsylvania Station—where he observes the city’s nocturnal glow and romanticizes strangers, until reconnecting with Jordan and learning she cheated in a golf tournament by moving her ball and lied about damaging a car, revealing her dishonesty and belief that others must accommodate her recklessness, leaving Nick emotionally detached due to an unresolved correspondence with a woman back home.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a chaotic, glittering party filled with guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, arriving by car and including a roster of over forty named figures such as Snell, Klipspringer, and Benny McClenahan, whose bizarre fates and gossip about Gatsby’s alleged crimes—bootlegging, murder, and ties to Von Hindenburg—highlight the hollow spectacle surrounding him. Later that day, Gatsby picks up Nick Carraway in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, driving to lunch while revealing an elaborate, inconsistent biography of Oxford education, wartime heroism in the Argonne Forest, and aristocratic European life, backed by physical proof: a Montenegrin medal inscribed 'Orderi di Danilo' and an Oxford photograph, before hinting at a 'big request' tied to Jordan Baker and using a white card to evade a speeding ticket. At noon in a cellar on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque underworld figure with cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and reveals Gatsby’s role in fixing the 1919 World Series; Gatsby abruptly leaves the table, and when Nick Carraway attempts to introduce him to Tom Buchanan, he vanishes. In a reflective flashback, Jordan Baker recounts her 1917 encounter with Daisy Fay and Lieutenant Gatsby in Louisville, Daisy’s drunken wedding day clutching a letter and demanding the $350,000 pearl necklace Tom gave her, her obsessive devotion to him until his car crash in 1919, their move to Chicago, and her 1920 childbirth, culminating in her sudden recognition of Gatsby’s name six weeks prior—prompting her to wake Nick Carraway at night. After leaving the Plaza Hotel, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy, having waited five years to ask him to arrange a tea invitation, fearing offense, and having spent years reading Chicago newspapers hoping to find her; as they ride through Central Park in a victoria at twilight, Nick Carraway shifts focus to Jordan, drawing her close with sudden personal attraction.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick returning home at two a.m. to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but deserted, with only wind causing the lights to flicker; Gatsby approaches him nervously, inviting him to Coney Island or a swim before awkwardly offering a side business opportunity. The next day, Nick calls Daisy to invite her for tea, warning her not to bring Tom, and heavy rain falls on the appointed day as Gatsby sends a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers. Daisy arrives by large open car with chauffeur Ferdie, and Gatsby, visibly shaken, nearly knocks over a mantelpiece clock during their stilted reunion, but soon they become calm and radiant with quiet joy. After the rain stops, Gatsby invites Daisy to tour his mansion, walking with her along the road rather than by the Sound; inside, they wander through opulent, empty rooms—Marie Antoinette music-rooms, Restoration Salons, and silk-swathed bedrooms—as Gatsby displays his collection of expensive shirts, causing Daisy to burst into tears over their beauty. Gatsby then shows Nick and Daisy a photograph of Mr. Dan Cody and a youthful picture of himself in yachting gear, which Daisy admires, and presents newspaper clippings about herself that they examine together; he is interrupted by a phone call about a misplaced guest from Detroit. As the rain clears, Daisy wistfully imagines placing Gatsby inside a pink cloud, and Gatsby summons Klipspringer, a boarder, to play piano, performing popular songs as thunder rumbles and electric trains run through the rain. Nick attempts to leave but is kept by their silent need for intimacy; as he departs, he sees Gatsby’s face darken with doubt, realizing Daisy cannot fulfill his idealized dream, while Gatsby clutches her hand, utterly absorbed in her voice, and Daisy glances at Nick one last time before they are lost to each other.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives unannounced at Gatsby’s mansion one morning seeking a statement about his mysterious background, confirming Gatsby’s notoriety; the narrative then traces Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, changed his name after encountering Dan Cody’s yacht anchored off Lake Superior, worked as a clam-digger and salmon-fisher along its shore, and was taken aboard Cody’s yacht the Tuolomee, where he served as steward, mate, skipper, secretary, and jailor for five years during transcontinental travels, only to be left with nothing after Cody’s death when Ella Kaye legally seized his entire fortune, leaving Gatsby with only the identity he had forged since adolescence. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby, visibly anxious, offers drinks and invites them to supper, but they politely refuse and depart, excluding him, while later at Gatsby’s party attended by Daisy and Tom, Tom grows suspicious of Gatsby’s origins and dismisses him as a possible bootlegger, Daisy is charmed by the spectacle yet disturbed by its rawness, and afterward Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway that Daisy did not enjoy the evening and insists he must recreate the exact moment five years ago when he first kissed her under moonlight to win her back. The chapter closes with Gatsby’s obsessive belief that the past can be repeated.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans' house to find Gatsby waiting; Gatsby has dismissed his original servants and replaced them with strangers linked to Wolfsheim. During lunch, Daisy kisses Gatsby in front of Tom, shocking him, and the group departs for New York in two cars—Tom forcing Gatsby to switch vehicles, with Tom driving Gatsby’s coupe and Gatsby driving Tom’s roadster, while Nick and Jordan ride with Tom. Tom interrogates Gatsby about his Oxford education and pink suit, dismissing his claims. The group stops at Wilson’s garage under the faded eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg, where Wilson, visibly ill and desperate for money, asks to buy Tom’s old car and hints at discovering Myrtle’s infidelity, unaware Tom plans to take her away; Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife and staring in jealous terror. At the Plaza Hotel, tensions erupt into a violent confrontation: Tom accuses Gatsby of being a bootlegger tied to Wolfsheim, while Gatsby demands Daisy admit she never loved Tom; Daisy reluctantly says she once loved Tom but still loves Gatsby, destroying Gatsby’s idealized dream. Tom declares Daisy will not leave him, and the couple departs in Gatsby’s blue coupe. Later, Michaelis finds George Wilson sick in his garage office, where Wilson reveals he has locked Myrtle upstairs and plans to move away; after Michaelis leaves briefly, Myrtle rushes out and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that does not stop. Tom and Nick arrive at the scene to find Myrtle’s body under a swinging yellow light; Wilson moans 'Oh, my God!' as Tom denies owning the yellow car, insisting his own is blue, and leaves the scene in tears, calling the driver a coward. That night, Nick waits outside the Buchanans’ house and Gatsby reveals Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle; Gatsby insists he will take the blame and spends the night watching her house, while Nick observes through the pantry window as Daisy and Tom sit together at the kitchen table, sharing chicken and ale in an unnervingly quiet, intimate silence.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby emotionally shattered after waiting all night for Daisy, who briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light. Inside the vast, dusty house, they smoke by the French windows as Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to avoid being implicated in Myrtle’s death, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the illusion that Daisy will choose him. He recounts his youth with Dan Cody and how he first fell in love with Daisy as a penniless officer, deliberately concealing his lack of wealth and family to win her affection, becoming irrevocably bound to her after taking her one October night. On the last afternoon before his departure, Gatsby shares a silent, tender moment with Daisy by a fire, realizing his ambitions mean nothing compared to her presence. Later, Gatsby revisits Louisville on foot after returning from war, walking their old paths and riding a hot day-coach away, desperately reaching for the fading memory of her as the sun sets. He never used his pool all summer; when Nick Carraway departs after missing two trains, he declares Gatsby worth more than Daisy and Tom combined, drawing a radiant smile from Gatsby in his pink suit. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and convinced the yellow car’s driver murdered Myrtle, travels on foot to Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, buys an uneaten sandwich and coffee, and is seen acting strangely by witnesses before arriving in West Egg and asking for Gatsby’s house. At two p.m., Gatsby dons his bathing suit, instructs the butler to bring calls to the pool, and carries a pneumatic mattress alone to the water—no call comes. The butler waits until four a.m., sensing Gatsby has abandoned his dream. The chauffeur hears gunshots but does not react; Nick Carraway arrives by car from the station and raises the alarm. Gatsby’s body is found floating in the pool on the mattress, and the gardener discovers Wilson’s body in the grass, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: In the aftermath of Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage a funeral attended by virtually no one, as police, reporters, and curious onlookers swarm the mansion while Daisy and Tom vanish without a trace; Meyer Wolfsheim refuses to attend, citing business and a personal aversion to death, and Klipspringer only requests his tennis shoes be mailed, while Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, devastated and awestruck by his son’s wealth, proudly displaying Gatsby’s childhood self-improvement schedule from a worn copy of Hopalong Cassidy; the funeral in the rain is attended only by Gatz, the Lutheran minister, Nick Carraway, and an unexpected visitor—the man with owl-eyed glasses—who, having last seen Gatsby marveling at his books, quietly mourns him as 'the poor son-of-a-bitch'; later, Nick Carraway confronts Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, where Tom admits he told George Wilson that Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary, and breaks down over dog biscuits left behind, revealing a hollow self-pity; after selling his car and erasing an obscene word scrawled on Gatsby’s steps, Nick Carraway visits the beach one final time, reflecting on the vanished natural beauty of the island and Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light, ending with the metaphor of humanity borne back ceaselessly into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Henry C. Gatz, Henry C. Gatz, recounts his journey into the world of Jay Gatsby through the eyes of Nick Carraway, a Yale acquaintance who moves to West Egg and becomes entangled in the lives of the wealthy elite. Nick rents a modest home near the opulent mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby, whose lavish parties draw crowds but conceal his true identity. Through Nick, Gatz learns that Gatsby’s wealth and spectacle are all orchestrated to win back Daisy Buchanan, Nick’s cousin, whom Gatsby loved five years prior as a penniless officer. Daisy, now married to the brutish and arrogant Tom Buchanan, lives across the bay in East Egg, and Gatsby’s entire life—his name, his fortune, even his Oxford education—has been meticulously constructed to bridge the gap between who he was and who he believes she still loves. Gatz, as Henry C. Gatz, pieces together this story from Nick’s observations, diary entries, and the testimonies of others, revealing Gatsby’s profound isolation beneath the glitter.

As summer unfolds, Nick becomes Gatsby’s reluctant confidant, facilitating a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy that initially seems to fulfill Gatsby’s dream. But the illusion shatters under Tom’s scrutiny, exposing Gatsby’s criminal ties through Meyer Wolfsheim and his fabricated aristocracy. The tension culminates on a sweltering afternoon at the Plaza Hotel, where Gatsby demands Daisy renounce her love for Tom; she falters, revealing she once loved Tom but now loves Gatsby too—a confession that destroys Gatsby’s idealized vision of her. That night, Daisy, driving Gatsby’s car, strikes and kills Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, who had been mistaking the car for Tom’s. Tom, in a calculated act of betrayal, tells Myrtle’s grieving husband George Wilson that Gatsby owned the vehicle. Gatsby, refusing to abandon his dream, takes the blame, spending the night watching Daisy’s house while she and Tom retreat into their hollow, intimate silence, untouched by consequence.

After Gatsby’s murder—gunned down in his pool by a grief-stricken Wilson, who then turns the gun on himself—Gatz, Henry C. Gatz, recounts the haunting emptiness of the aftermath. Daisy and Tom vanish without a trace; Gatsby’s so-called friends, including Wolfsheim and Klipspringer, disappear or offer only petty requests. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives from Minnesota, carrying his son’s childhood self-improvement schedule as proof of the boy’s boundless ambition. At the sparse funeral, attended by Nick, a minister, and the owl-eyed man who once marveled at Gatsby’s real books, Gatz reflects on the tragic irony: his son died believing in a dream that never existed, yet was more noble than the careless people who destroyed him. In the final moments, Gatz, alive and whole, walks the beach where Gatsby once reached for the green light, now extinguished, and understands that humanity, like Gatsby, is forever chasing a past it cannot reclaim.
